title: Supreme Court Finds Prima Facie Contempt in Delhi Protest Curbs, Seeks Compliance Affidavit, Adjourns to October 15
excerpt: A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana directed that metro and rail services run normally, barricades be reviewed forthwith, internet services remain undisturbed, and the Section 163 board near the court be taken down — then issued notice on the contempt plea.
body:
• The Supreme Court on Tuesday found a case of "prima facie" contempt in the authorities' handling of the Delhi protest restrictions and issued notice, seeking responses along with a compliance affidavit on its earlier directions.
  • The bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana directed that metro and rail facilities function normally unless restrictions are justified under Article 19(2), that free movement in the city be permitted, and that barricades be reviewed forthwith.
  • Internet services are to remain undisturbed, and the board announcing Section 163 BNSS restrictions around the Supreme Court is to be taken down so access to justice is not impeded.
  • The matter — arising from protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR voter-roll exercise — was adjourned to October 15, with Justice Mohana unwell.

The Supreme Court tightened its hold on the Delhi protest case on Tuesday, telling the authorities it sees a prima facie case of contempt in how its earlier directions on transport shutdowns and detentions were handled. A bench of Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana issued notice on the contempt plea and sought the authorities' response together with a compliance affidavit on the earlier directions regarding train and metro services, Live Law reported.

What the bench ordered this time

The directions were specific. Metro and rail facilities are to function normally unless restrictions are required keeping in mind disturbances to public order, as contemplated under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Free movement in the city is to be permitted subject to traffic regulations, and lawyers, journalists and other professionals are not to be impeded in discharging their professional duties. The imposition of barricades is to be reviewed forthwith, keeping law and order and traffic conditions in mind. Internet services are to remain undisturbed. And the board concerning the imposition of Section 163 of the BNSS in the area around the Supreme Court is to be taken down, if not already done, so there is no apprehension regarding access to justice — including ingress and egress to any court of law.

https://x.com/TheQuint/status/2109613254133891151

How the case reached contempt

The litigation began when CPI(M) General Secretary M.A. Baby and other petitioners challenged the curbs imposed ahead of protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls. On October 9, hearing complaints that 57 metro stations had been closed and long-distance trains cancelled, the court drew the line that has governed the case since: authorities may regulate movement, but they may not impose a complete prohibition on public transport. A contempt petition followed, alleging officials failed to comply with those limits during the October 10 demonstrations and the opposition's planned march to the court on October 12 — when the Chief Justice orally remarked that democratic activities should take place at designated places and the Supreme Court should not be dragged into such things, while affirming every lawyer's right to take part in a peaceful protest.

The matter was adjourned to October 15, with Justice Mohana unwell. The compliance affidavit due by then will show whether the authorities treated the court's directions as binding limits or as advice — which is precisely what the contempt proceeding exists to decide.
